claim: In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), more than 50% of cases display autoactivation of Notch1 signaling.
source: In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), more than 50% of cases display autoactivation of Notch1 signaling, leading to oncogenic transformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about T-ALL and is stated in the abstract.

claim: Autoactivation of Notch1 signaling leads to oncogenic transformation in T-ALL.
source: In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), more than 50% of cases display autoactivation of Notch1 signaling, leading to oncogenic transformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the role of Notch1 in T-ALL.

claim: A specific chemovar of Cannabis induces apoptosis by preventing Notch1 maturation in leukemia cells.
source: We have previously identified a specific chemovar of Cannabis that induces apoptosis by preventing Notch1 maturation in leukemia cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Three cannabinoids were isolated from a Cannabis chemovar that synergistically mimic the effects of the whole extract.
source: Here, we isolated three cannabinoids from this chemovar that synergistically mimic the effects of the whole extract.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1.

claim: Two of the isolated cannabinoids are cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabidivarin (CBDV).
source: Two were previously known, cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabidivarin (CBDV), whereas the third cannabinoid, which we termed 331-18A, was identified and fully characterized in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from phytocannabinoid analysis and isolation procedures.

claim: The third cannabinoid was termed 331-18A and was identified and fully characterized in this study.
source: Two were previously known, cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabidivarin (CBDV), whereas the third cannabinoid, which we termed 331-18A, was identified and fully characterized in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry presented in Figure 1 and supplementary materials.

claim: The three cannabinoids act through cannabinoid receptor type 2 (CB2) and TRPV1.
source: We demonstrated that these cannabinoids act through cannabinoid receptor type 2 and TRPV1 to activate the integrated stress response pathway by depleting intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using receptor antagonists shown in Figure 2.

claim: The cannabinoids activate the integrated stress response pathway by depleting intracellular Ca2+.
source: We demonstrated that these cannabinoids act through cannabinoid receptor type 2 and TRPV1 to activate the integrated stress response pathway by depleting intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Treatment with the cannabinoids increases mRNA and protein expression of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1.
source: This is followed by increased mRNA and protein expression of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1, which is hindered by inhibiting the upstream initiation factor eIF2α.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR and western blot analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increased expression of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1 is hindered by inhibiting the upstream initiation factor eIF2α.
source: This is followed by increased mRNA and protein expression of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1, which is hindered by inhibiting the upstream initiation factor eIF2α.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using ISRIB inhibitor shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increased abundance of CHAC1 prevents Notch1 maturation.
source: The increased abundance of CHAC1 prevents Notch1 maturation, thereby reducing the levels of the active Notch1 intracellular domain, and consequently decreasing cell viability and increasing apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the integrated stress response pathway activation shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Prevention of Notch1 maturation reduces the levels of the active Notch1 intracellular domain (NICD).
source: The increased abundance of CHAC1 prevents Notch1 maturation, thereby reducing the levels of the active Notch1 intracellular domain, and consequently decreasing cell viability and increasing apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analysis of NICD shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Reduction of NICD levels decreases cell viability and increases apoptosis.
source: The increased abundance of CHAC1 prevents Notch1 maturation, thereby reducing the levels of the active Notch1 intracellular domain, and consequently decreasing cell viability and increasing apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from viability assays and apoptosis measurements shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Treatment with the three isolated molecules resulted in reduced tumor size and weight in vivo.
source: Treatment with the three isolated molecules resulted in reduced tumor size and weight in vivo and slowed leukemia progression in mice models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse xenograft models shown in Figure 6.

claim: Treatment with the three isolated molecules slowed leukemia progression in mice models.
source: Treatment with the three isolated molecules resulted in reduced tumor size and weight in vivo and slowed leukemia progression in mice models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intravenous leukemia models shown in Figure 6.

claim: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive cancer characterized by immature T-lymphoblasts.
source: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive cancer, characterized by immature T-lymphoblasts (Girardi et al., 2017; Vadillo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In over 50% of T-ALL cases, activating mutations in NOTCH1 were identified.
source: In over 50% of cases, activating mutations in NOTCH1 were identified, generating much interest in targeting the Notch1 signaling pathway in this disease (Sorrentino et al., 2019; Ferrando, 2009; McCarter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Notch1 protein is a single-pass transmembrane receptor expressed on the plasma membrane.
source: The Notch1 protein is a single-pass transmembrane receptor that is expressed on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch1 structure.

claim: Notch1 regulates evolutionarily conserved signaling that controls developmental processes, cell fate determination, and tissue homeostasis.
source: It regulates evolutionarily conserved signaling that controls developmental processes, cell fate determination, and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Notch1 is a member of the Notch receptor family, which consists of four receptors (Notch1-4) in humans.
source: It is a member of the Notch receptor family, which consists of four receptors (Notch1-4) in humans (Ferrando, 2009; Fang-Fang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Notch1 receptor-signaling pathway is activated through a series of proteolytic cleavages at three different sites (S1–S3).
source: The Notch1 receptor-signaling pathway is activated through a series of proteolytic cleavages at three different sites (S1–S3).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch1 activation.

claim: S1 cleavage is carried out by a Furin-like convertase in the trans-Golgi apparatus.
source: S1 cleavage is carried out by a Furin-like convertase in the trans-Golgi apparatus, resulting in a heterodimeric receptor that is transported to the membrane where it can bind ligands from a neighboring cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch1 processing.

claim: S1 cleavage results in a heterodimeric receptor that is transported to the membrane where it can bind ligands from a neighboring cell.
source: S1 cleavage is carried out by a Furin-like convertase in the trans-Golgi apparatus, resulting in a heterodimeric receptor that is transported to the membrane where it can bind ligands from a neighboring cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch1 processing.

claim: Upon ligand binding, cleavage at the next site initiates the activation of the Notch1 receptor-signaling pathway.
source: Upon binding of a ligand, cleavage is performed at the next site and the activation of the Notch1 receptor-signaling pathway is initiated, enabling the cleavage of S3 in the transmembrane region that causes the release of the Notch1 intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus where it promotes transcription of target genes involved in cell growth (Katoh and Katoh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: S3 cleavage in the transmembrane region causes the release of the Notch1 intracellular domain (NICD).
source: Upon binding of a ligand, cleavage is performed at the next site and the activation of the Notch1 receptor-signaling pathway is initiated, enabling the cleavage of S3 in the transmembrane region that causes the release of the Notch1 intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus where it promotes transcription of target genes involved in cell growth (Katoh and Katoh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NICD translocates to the nucleus where it promotes transcription of target genes involved in cell growth.
source: Upon binding of a ligand, cleavage is performed at the next site and the activation of the Notch1 receptor-signaling pathway is initiated, enabling the cleavage of S3 in the transmembrane region that causes the release of the Notch1 intracellular domain (NICD), which translocates to the nucleus where it promotes transcription of target genes involved in cell growth (Katoh and Katoh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Aberrant Notch1 activity is associated with many other leukemia types and other cancers, including prostate, lung, ovarian, and renal.
source: Aberrant Notch1 activity is associated with many other leukemia types and other cancers, including prostate, lung, ovarian, and renal (Qiu et al., 2018; Rice et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Kahn et al., 2018; Vinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The endocannabinoid system (eCBS) is a ubiquitous neuromodulatory signaling system that has widespread functions throughout the body.
source: Phytocannabinoids affect the body by means of the endocannabinoid system (eCBS), a ubiquitous neuromodulatory signaling system that has widespread functions throughout the body.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the endocannabinoid system.

claim: Notable eCBS receptors include cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1) and CB2, which belong to the family of G protein-coupled receptors.
source: Notable eCBS receptors include cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1) and CB2, which belong to the family of G protein-coupled receptors, and transient receptor potential vanilloid type 1 (TRPV1), which is an ion channel (Punzo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: TRPV1 is an ion channel that is part of the eCBS.
source: Notable eCBS receptors include cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1) and CB2, which belong to the family of G protein-coupled receptors, and transient receptor potential vanilloid type 1 (TRPV1), which is an ion channel (Punzo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The eCBS participates in many physiological activities, including the regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis.
source: The eCBS participates in many physiological activities, including the regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis (Jeon et al., 2023; Muller et al., 2018; Laguerre et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Medical Cannabis is commonly used by cancer patients for its palliative effects.
source: Medical Cannabis is already commonly used by cancer patients for its palliative effects, it was shown to stimulate appetite while alleviating symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and pain (Abrams and Guzman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cannabis stimulates appetite while alleviating symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and pain.
source: Medical Cannabis is already commonly used by cancer patients for its palliative effects, it was shown to stimulate appetite while alleviating symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and pain (Abrams and Guzman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Phytocannabinoids directly affect tumor development in cell lines and animal models by modulating key cell-signaling pathways.
source: However, accumulating evidence demonstrated phytocannabinoids directly affect tumor development in cell lines and animal models by modulating key cell-signaling pathways (Abrams, 2016; Duran et al., 2010; Pagano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Purified phytocannabinoids can inhibit proliferation, metastasis, and angiogenesis in a variety of cancer cell types.
source: Studies demonstrated that purified phytocannabinoids can inhibit proliferation, metastasis, and angiogenesis and exert pro-apoptotic effects in a variety of cancer cell types such as lung, breast, prostate, skin, intestine, glioma, lymphoma, pancreas, and uterine cancers (Kovalchuk and Kovalchuk, 2020; O'Reilly et al., 2022; Blázquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Purified phytocannabinoids exert pro-apoptotic effects in a variety of cancer cell types.
source: Studies demonstrated that purified phytocannabinoids can inhibit proliferation, metastasis, and angiogenesis and exert pro-apoptotic effects in a variety of cancer cell types such as lung, breast, prostate, skin, intestine, glioma, lymphoma, pancreas, and uterine cancers (Kovalchuk and Kovalchuk, 2020; O'Reilly et al., 2022; Blázquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In preclinical models, treatment with phytocannabinoids led to tumor regression of different cancer types.
source: In preclinical models, treatment with phytocannabinoids led to tumor regression of different cancer types (McAllister et al., 2015; Hinz and Ramer, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Studies using phytocannabinoids and their formulations have shown anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects in selected leukemia cell lines and native leukemia blasts cultured ex vivo.
source: Concerning T-ALL, some studies using phytocannabinoids and their respective formulations (such as dronabinol) have shown anti-proliferative as well as pro-apoptotic effects in selected leukemia cell lines and native leukemia blasts cultured ex vivo (Kampa-Schittenhelm et al., 2016; Scott et al., 2017; Olivas-Aguirre et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mechanisms of phytocannabinoid-mediated antitumor effects are not yet fully understood.
source: Nevertheless, the mechanisms of phytocannabinoid-mediated antitumor effects are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the state of the literature.

claim: More than 140 different phytocannabinoids have been identified in different Cannabis chemovars.
source: Most of the studies that examined the anti-cancer effects of Cannabis have focused mainly on the two major phytocannabinoids (−)-trans-Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), but these are just two of more than 140 different phytocannabinoids that have been identified in different Cannabis chemovars (Berman et al., 2018; Hanuš et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Different Cannabis extracts with unique phytocannabinoid compositions impaired the survival and proliferation of specific cancer cell lines.
source: We have previously demonstrated that different Cannabis extracts with unique phytocannabinoid compositions impaired the survival and proliferation of specific cancer cell lines, suggesting that the effect of a particular Cannabis extract on a specific cancer cell line relies on its chemical composition (Baram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The effect of a particular Cannabis extract on a specific cancer cell line relies on its chemical composition.
source: We have previously demonstrated that different Cannabis extracts with unique phytocannabinoid compositions impaired the survival and proliferation of specific cancer cell lines, suggesting that the effect of a particular Cannabis extract on a specific cancer cell line relies on its chemical composition (Baram et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors and inference from their data.

claim: A specific CBD-rich Cannabis extract was successfully matched to T-ALL leukemia cells that harbor a NOTCH1 mutation.
source: Following this framework, we successfully matched a specific CBD-rich Cannabis extract to T-ALL leukemia cells that harbor a NOTCH1 mutation (Besser et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A specific CBD-rich Cannabis extract selectively induces apoptosis in T-ALL leukemia cell lines that harbor a NOTCH1 mutation.
source: We have previously shown a specific CBD-rich Cannabis extract selectively induces apoptosis in T-ALL leukemia cell lines that harbor a NOTCH1 mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Treatment with the CBD-rich extract led to accumulation of the full-length immature form of Notch1 in the membrane.
source: Treatment led to accumulation of the full-length immature form of Notch1 in the membrane, correspondingly with reduced NICD protein expression and transcription activity (Besser et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Treatment with the CBD-rich extract resulted in reduced NICD protein expression and transcription activity.
source: Treatment led to accumulation of the full-length immature form of Notch1 in the membrane, correspondingly with reduced NICD protein expression and transcription activity (Besser et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The CBD-rich extract was more potent than pure CBD or other high-CBD chemovars.
source: The CBD-rich extract was more potent than pure CBD or other high-CBD chemovars (Besser et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A specific combination of metabolites from the plant potentiate the full antitumor effect of the CBD-rich extract.
source: This implied a specific combination of metabolites from the plant potentiate the full antitumor effect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the whole extract is more potent than pure CBD.

claim: Fraction 2 reduced viability of MOLT-4 cells to a similar extent as the whole extract.
source: We assessed the effect of each fraction on the viability of MOLT-4 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and found fraction 2 reduced viability to a similar extent as the whole extract.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only fraction 2 induced apoptotic cell death.
source: Further analysis revealed that out of the four fractions, only fraction 2 induced apoptotic cell death (Figure 1B), reduced the protein levels of the NICD (Figure 1C and D) and elevated the levels of cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fraction 2 reduced the protein levels of NICD.
source: Further analysis revealed that out of the four fractions, only fraction 2 induced apoptotic cell death (Figure 1B), reduced the protein levels of the NICD (Figure 1C and D) and elevated the levels of cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Fraction 2 elevated the levels of cleaved caspase-3.
source: Further analysis revealed that out of the four fractions, only fraction 2 induced apoptotic cell death (Figure 1B), reduced the protein levels of the NICD (Figure 1C and D) and elevated the levels of cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: C1 was identified as 331-18A, a phytocannabinoid first identified by the authors in decarboxylated CBD-rich Cannabis chemovars.
source: C1 was identified as 331-18A, a phytocannabinoid first identified by our team in decarboxylated CBD-rich Cannabis chemovars (Berman et al., 2018), we characterized 331-18A using ESI-LC-MS/MS as having a deprotonated m/z of 331.2279 and MS/MS fragments resembling those of CBD with the addition of one hydroxyl group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry and citation to previous work.

claim: 331-18A has a deprotonated m/z of 331.2279.
source: C1 was identified as 331-18A, a phytocannabinoid first identified by our team in decarboxylated CBD-rich Cannabis chemovars (Berman et al., 2018), we characterized 331-18A using ESI-LC-MS/MS as having a deprotonated m/z of 331.2279 and MS/MS fragments resembling those of CBD with the addition of one hydroxyl group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry.

claim: 331-18A has MS/MS fragments resembling those of CBD with the addition of one hydroxyl group.
source: C1 was identified as 331-18A, a phytocannabinoid first identified by our team in decarboxylated CBD-rich Cannabis chemovars (Berman et al., 2018), we characterized 331-18A using ESI-LC-MS/MS as having a deprotonated m/z of 331.2279 and MS/MS fragments resembling those of CBD with the addition of one hydroxyl group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry.

claim: The NMR spectra of CBD and 331-18A were very similar with the exception of the disappearance of the external double bond (C8-C10) and the appearance of a tertiary alcohol instead.
source: The spectra of CBD and 331-18A were very similar with the exception of the disappearance of the external double bond (C8-C10) and the appearance of a tertiary alcohol instead.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 1 and supplementary materials.

claim: The absolute stereochemistry of 331-18A was confirmed by specific rotation determination with a polarimeter.
source: The absolute stereochemistry of 331-18A was confirmed by specific rotation determination with a polarimeter in which 331-18A showed [α]20D −56.85 which is comparable with the [α]20D −64.16 of both the CBD that was isolated from the fraction (C5) and a commercial standard of CBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from polarimetry.

claim: 331-18A showed [α]20D −56.85 which is comparable with the [α]20D −64.16 of CBD.
source: The absolute stereochemistry of 331-18A was confirmed by specific rotation determination with a polarimeter in which 331-18A showed [α]20D −56.85 which is comparable with the [α]20D −64.16 of both the CBD that was isolated from the fraction (C5) and a commercial standard of CBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from polarimetry.

claim: The two substituents at positions 1 and 6 of the cyclohexene ring in 331-18A are in a trans configuration, similarly to CBD.
source: These results suggested that similarly to CBD, the two substituents at positions 1 and 6 of the cyclohexene ring are in a trans configuration (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the polarimetry data and comparison with CBD structure.

claim: 331-18A and CBDV alone did not induce apoptosis or had minor effects on MOLT-4 cells.
source: Compared to the whole extract, the phytocannabinoids 331-18A and CBDV alone did not induce apoptosis or had minor effects on the cells, and CBD alone induced only 55% cell death compared to the whole extract (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CBD alone induced only 55% cell death compared to the whole extract.
source: Compared to the whole extract, the phytocannabinoids 331-18A and CBDV alone did not induce apoptosis or had minor effects on the cells, and CBD alone induced only 55% cell death compared to the whole extract (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: When CBD was combined with either 331-18A or CBDV, the percent of apoptotic cells increased to 58% and 61%, respectively.
source: When CBD was combined with either 331-18A or CBDV, the percent of apoptotic cells increased to 58% and 61%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The combination of all three phytocannabinoids led to the greatest cytotoxic effect.
source: The combination of all three phytocannabinoids led to the greatest cytotoxic effect and only this combination was comparable to the whole extract (88.29% ± 4.31% and 93.85% ± 1.64%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Only the combination of all three cannabinoids was comparable to the whole extract in inducing apoptosis (88.29% ± 4.31% and 93.85% ± 1.64%, respectively).
source: The combination of all three phytocannabinoids led to the greatest cytotoxic effect and only this combination was comparable to the whole extract (88.29% ± 4.31% and 93.85% ± 1.64%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: All combinations of phytocannabinoids led to a significant reduction in NICD expression.
source: We further evaluated the effect of the three phytocannabinoids separately or in different combinations on the protein expression of NICD (Figure 1H and I, Figure 1—source data 2) and found that all combinations of phytocannabinoids led to a significant reduction in NICD expression, but only when all the three were combined, NICD levels decreased to the same extent as with the whole extract.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Only when all three cannabinoids were combined, NICD levels decreased to the same extent as with the whole extract.
source: We further evaluated the effect of the three phytocannabinoids separately or in different combinations on the protein expression of NICD (Figure 1H and I, Figure 1—source data 2) and found that all combinations of phytocannabinoids led to a significant reduction in NICD expression, but only when all the three were combined, NICD levels decreased to the same extent as with the whole extract.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: MOLT-4 cells have low expression of CNR1, TRPA1, and TRPM8.
source: The ΔCT results showed low expression for CNR1, TRPA1, and TRPM8, medium expression for CNR2 and GPR55, and high expression for TRPV1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MOLT-4 cells have medium expression of CNR2 and GPR55.
source: The ΔCT results showed low expression for CNR1, TRPA1, and TRPM8, medium expression for CNR2 and GPR55, and high expression for TRPV1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MOLT-4 cells have high expression of TRPV1.
source: The ΔCT results showed low expression for CNR1, TRPA1, and TRPM8, medium expression for CNR2 and GPR55, and high expression for TRPV1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only the CB2 and TRPV1 antagonists rescued the expression of NICD upon treatment with the whole extract.
source: We tested antagonists for those receptors that had either high or medium expression: TRPV1 (AMG9810), CB2 (AM630 or SR-144,528), GPR55 (CID), and general Gq GPCR (BIM-46187) as a control, and evaluated whether they were able to rescue NICD expression upon treatment with the whole extract (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1). Only the CB2 and TRPV1 antagonists rescued the expression of NICD upon treatment with the whole extract, therefore we tested whether they were able to rescue NICD expression after treatment with the combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The CB2 antagonist rescued NICD expression from 56% to 87% upon treatment with the cannabinoid combination.
source: The CB2 antagonist rescued the expression from 56% to 87%, and the TRPV1 antagonist rescued NICD expression to 100% by itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The TRPV1 antagonist rescued NICD expression to 100% by itself upon treatment with the cannabinoid combination.
source: The CB2 antagonist rescued the expression from 56% to 87%, and the TRPV1 antagonist rescued NICD expression to 100% by itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Each of the cannabinoids separately caused some elevation in Ca2+.
source: We used the Fluo-4 calcium probe to measure the effect of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD combination on MOLT-4. Each of the molecules separately caused some elevation in Ca2+, but only their combination had an effect on Ca2+ to the same extent as the whole extract (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only the combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD had an effect on Ca2+ to the same extent as the whole extract.
source: We used the Fluo-4 calcium probe to measure the effect of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD combination on MOLT-4. Each of the molecules separately caused some elevation in Ca2+, but only their combination had an effect on Ca2+ to the same extent as the whole extract (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both CB2 and TRPV1 antagonists inhibited the Ca2+ elevation in response to the whole extract.
source: We tested Ca2+ levels when cells were pretreated with the antagonists to CB2 and TRPV1. Both antagonists inhibited the elevation in response to the whole extract (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: CB2 but not TRPV1 antagonist diminished 331-18A induced Ca2+ increase, indicating this cannabinoid exerts its effect through CB2.
source: When 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD were tested separately with antagonists to either CB2 or TRPV1 (Figure 2E), CB2 but not TRPV1 antagonist diminished 331-18A induced Ca2+ increase, indicating this cannabinoid exerts its effect through CB2, while both antagonists significantly decreased the Ca2+ elevation by CBDV and CBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and inference from the antagonist effects.

claim: Both CB2 and TRPV1 antagonists significantly decreased the Ca2+ elevation by CBDV and CBD.
source: When 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD were tested separately with antagonists to either CB2 or TRPV1 (Figure 2E), CB2 but not TRPV1 antagonist diminished 331-18A induced Ca2+ increase, indicating this cannabinoid exerts its effect through CB2, while both antagonists significantly decreased the Ca2+ elevation by CBDV and CBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Inhibition of CB2 only partially rescued MOLT-4 cells from treatment-induced apoptosis, reducing the apoptotic rate from 75% to 40%.
source: Upon treatment with the combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD, inhibition of CB2 only partially rescued the cells from treatment-induced apoptosis, reducing the apoptotic rate from 75% of the combination-treated cells to 40%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Inhibition of TRPV1 only partially rescued MOLT-4 cells from treatment-induced apoptosis to ~50%.
source: Inhibition of TRPV1 only also partially rescued the cells, to ~50%, but again the apoptotic rate remained significantly increased relative to the untreated control.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Inhibition of both CB2 and TRPV1 simultaneously rescued MOLT-4 cells from treatment-induced apoptosis.
source: Inhibition of both CB2 and TRPV1 simultaneously rescued the cells from treatment-induced apoptosis, confirming the effect of the three cannabinoids is mediated through both receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The effect of the three cannabinoids is mediated through both CB2 and TRPV1 receptors.
source: Inhibition of both CB2 and TRPV1 simultaneously rescued the cells from treatment-induced apoptosis, confirming the effect of the three cannabinoids is mediated through both receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and inference from the rescue experiments.

claim: CHAC1 was identified as the second most increased-abundance gene following treatment with the whole extract.
source: ChaC glutathione-specific γ-glutamylcyclotransferase 1 (CHAC1), a negative regulator of the Notch signaling pathway (Chen et al., 2017), was identified as the second most increased-abundance gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Affymetrix analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CHAC1 is a negative regulator of the Notch signaling pathway.
source: ChaC glutathione-specific γ-glutamylcyclotransferase 1 (CHAC1), a negative regulator of the Notch signaling pathway (Chen et al., 2017), was identified as the second most increased-abundance gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHAC1 acts by inhibiting the furin-like cleavage of Notch1, preventing the formation of the mature form of Notch1.
source: CHAC1 acts by inhibiting the furin-like cleavage of Notch1, preventing the formation of the mature form of Notch1 (Chi et al., 2012), as we have previously demonstrated upon treatment with the whole extract (Besser et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and previous work by the authors.

claim: The gene DDIT3 that encodes CHOP and ATF4 had a significant increase in their abundance following treatment.
source: The gene DDIT3 that encodes C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), ER-stress signaling pathway markers that are upstream to CHAC1 (Joo et al., 2015), had also a significant increase in their abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Affymetrix analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATF4 and CHOP are ER-stress signaling pathway markers that are upstream to CHAC1.
source: The gene DDIT3 that encodes C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), ER-stress signaling pathway markers that are upstream to CHAC1 (Joo et al., 2015), had also a significant increase in their abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mRNA of ATF4, DDIT3, and CHAC1 is significantly increased after treatment with a combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD.
source: We confirmed the Affymetrix results by qRT-PCR showing that the mRNA of ATF4, DDIT3, and CHAC1 is indeed significantly increased after treatment with a combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD (Figure 3B–D, respectively) or the whole extract (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: A significant increase in ATF4, DDIT3, and CHAC1 mRNA was apparent 60 min after treatment.
source: A significant increase was apparent 60 min after treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The protein expression level of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1 was significantly increased at 60 min after treatment.
source: Using specific antibodies to ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1, we verified the protein expression level of all three was also significantly increased at 60 min after treatment (Figure 3E–H, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analysis shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: The protein expression levels of CHAC1 in MOLT-4 cells were significantly increased upon treatment with the whole extract.
source: The protein expression levels of CHAC1 in MOLT-4 cells were also significantly increased upon treatment with the whole extract (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Inhibition of CB2 reduced the treatment-induced increase in mRNA expression of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1.
source: To further understand the mechanism, we evaluated how pretreatment with antagonists to the cannabinoid receptors through which 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD exert their effect, CB2 and TRPV1, affected ATF4, DDIT3, and CHAC1 expression following treatment (Figure 3I–K). Inhibition of CB2 reduced the treatment-induced increase in mRNA expression, but a trend of increase for ATF4 and CHOP remained at 60 min, and CHAC1 expression was significantly increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Inhibition of TRPV1 rescued from treatment-induced induction of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1.
source: Inhibition of TRPV1 rescued from treatment-induced induction of all three targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: The increase in the expression levels of CHAC1 protein was abolished when MOLT-4 cells were treated with either CB2 or TRPV1 antagonist.
source: Similar effects were found when pretreatment with antagonists to CB2 and TRPV1 was followed by treatment with the whole extract (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H); and the increase in the expression levels of CHAC1 protein was abolished when MOLT-4 cells were treated by either antagonist (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: CB2 and TRPV1 participate in inducing CHAC1 expression and preventing Notch1 maturation.
source: These results demonstrate that CB2 and TRPV1 participate in inducing CHAC1 expression and preventing Notch1 maturation, resulting in a decrease in NICD release and cell death.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that antagonists to these receptors prevent CHAC1 induction and rescue NICD expression.

claim: The combination of the three cannabinoids causes the activation of ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 signaling by Ca2+ depletion and ER stress.
source: We therefore speculated that the combination of the three cannabinoids caused the activation of ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 signaling by Ca2+ depletion and ER stress (Zhai et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data and citation to published literature.

claim: Blocking the activity of eIF2α with ISRIB prevented the cytotoxic effect of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD combination.
source: Then, we treated the cells with either vehicle or the combination of the cannabinoids. After 24 hr, blocking the activity of eIF2α prevented the cytotoxic effect of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD combination (Figure 4A) or of the whole extract (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: eIF2α inhibition prevented the reduction in NICD expression upon treatment with the cannabinoid combination.
source: Moreover, eIF2α inhibition prevented the reduction in NICD expression upon treatment with either the whole extract (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 2) or the cannabinoid combination (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Inhibition of eIF2α rescued the cells from the induced increase in the mRNA expression of ATF4, DDIT3 (CHOP), and CHAC1 upon treatment with the combination of the cannabinoids.
source: Inhibition of eIF2α also rescued the cells from the induced increase in the mRNA expression of ATF4, DDIT3 (CHOP), and CHAC1 upon treatment with the combination of the cannabinoids (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Inhibition of the integrated stress response pathway rescued MOLT-4 cells from the cytotoxic effect of the combination of the three cannabinoids.
source: Thus, inhibition of the integrated stress response pathway, eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 signaling, rescued MOLT-4 cells from the cytotoxic effect of the combination of the three cannabinoids and prevented the reduction in NICD expression, as well as the increased transcription of ATF4, CHOP, and CHAC1 upon treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and inference from the rescue experiments.

claim: 331-18A affected viability of MOLT-4 cells from a dose of 1 µg/mL.
source: First we tested the ability of each separate cannabinoid to inhibit the proliferation of MOLT-4 cells in doses ranging 0–2 µg/mL (Figure 5A), which is below and above the overall concentration for which we found an effect for the cannabinoid combination. 331-18A and CBDV affected viability from a dose of 1 µg/mL and CBD from a dose of 0.5 µg/mL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CBDV affected viability of MOLT-4 cells from a dose of 1 µg/mL.
source: First we tested the ability of each separate cannabinoid to inhibit the proliferation of MOLT-4 cells in doses ranging 0–2 µg/mL (Figure 5A), which is below and above the overall concentration for which we found an effect for the cannabinoid combination. 331-18A and CBDV affected viability from a dose of 1 µg/mL and CBD from a dose of 0.5 µg/mL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CBD affected viability of MOLT-4 cells from a dose of 0.5 µg/mL.
source: First we tested the ability of each separate cannabinoid to inhibit the proliferation of MOLT-4 cells in doses ranging 0–2 µg/mL (Figure 5A), which is below and above the overall concentration for which we found an effect for the cannabinoid combination. 331-18A and CBDV affected viability from a dose of 1 µg/mL and CBD from a dose of 0.5 µg/mL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A combination of CBDV with either 331-18A or CBD results in a likely antagonistic interaction according to HSA reference model.
source: According to Highest Single Agent (HSA) reference model (Yadav et al., 2015), a combination of CBDV with either 331-18A or CBD results in a likely antagonistic interaction (score < –10), a combination of 331-18A and CBD results in a likely additive interaction (score from –10 to 10), and only the combination of all three cannabinoids is likely synergistic (score >10, Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and synergy analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A combination of 331-18A and CBD results in a likely additive interaction according to HSA reference model.
source: According to Highest Single Agent (HSA) reference model (Yadav et al., 2015), a combination of CBDV with either 331-18A or CBD results in a likely antagonistic interaction (score < –10), a combination of 331-18A and CBD results in a likely additive interaction (score from –10 to 10), and only the combination of all three cannabinoids is likely synergistic (score >10, Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and synergy analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only the combination of all three cannabinoids is likely synergistic according to HSA reference model.
source: According to Highest Single Agent (HSA) reference model (Yadav et al., 2015), a combination of CBDV with either 331-18A or CBD results in a likely antagonistic interaction (score < –10), a combination of 331-18A and CBD results in a likely additive interaction (score from –10 to 10), and only the combination of all three cannabinoids is likely synergistic (score >10, Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and synergy analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment with a combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD significantly inhibited tumor growth in a subcutaneous tumor model.
source: We engrafted subcutaneously nonobese diabetic-severe combined immunodeficiency (NOD/Scid) mice with MOLT-4 cells, then treated with vehicle only or the combination of the cannabinoids from when tumors reached a volume of 100 mm3 (day 7), on alternating days, for a duration of 4 weeks. Treatment with a combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD significantly inhibited tumor growth (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse xenograft models shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Significant differences in tumor volume were apparent approximately 3 weeks after treatment started.
source: Significant differences were apparent approximately 3 weeks after treatment started (Figure 6A), and at the endpoint, 34 days from the injection of cells, the average weight of tumors was significantly lower in the treated group compared to the control group (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At the endpoint (34 days from cell injection), the average weight of tumors was significantly lower in the treated group compared to the control group.
source: Significant differences were apparent approximately 3 weeks after treatment started (Figure 6A), and at the endpoint, 34 days from the injection of cells, the average weight of tumors was significantly lower in the treated group compared to the control group (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The three cannabinoids were identified and quantified in the tumors at concentrations of 16.0±6.7, 22.3±10.4, and 265.8±109.7 ng/g for CBDV, 331-18A, and CBD, respectively.
source: Using ESI-LC/MS, we identified and quantified each of the three cannabinoids in the tumors (16.0±6.7, 22.3±10.4, and 265.8±109.7 ng/g for CBDV, 331-18A, and CBD, respectively [average ± SEM, N=3]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis of tumor tissue.

claim: The ratio of the cannabinoids analyzed in the tumors was similar to the ratio given to the mice in the treatment protocol.
source: Notably, the ratio of the cannabinoids analyzed in the tumors was similar to the ratio given to the mice in the treatment protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis of tumor tissue.

claim: A significant decrease was observed in NICD expression in the tumors treated with the cannabinoids.
source: In addition, a significant decrease was observed in NICD expression in the tumors treated with the cannabinoids (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There were no significant differences in the average weight of mice in the control group and the treatment group in the subcutaneous tumor model.
source: To assess possible toxicity, the body weight of the mice was monitored throughout the experiment (Figure 6E). There were no significant differences in the average weight of mice in the control group and the treatment group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The amount of human CD45+ cells detected in the bone marrow was significantly decreased in mice treated with the combination of the three cannabinoids compared to the control in the intravenous leukemia model.
source: We engrafted NOD/Scid IL2rγ-null (NSG) mice that are a better host for human immune cells with CCRF-CEM, Notch1-mutated T-ALL cells. The mice were treated with a combination of the three cannabinoids, and to verify the need for the combination, one group was also treated with pure CBD in the same overall dose. At the endpoint of the experiment, the amount of human CD45+ cells detected in the bone marrow (BM) was significantly decreased in the mice treated with the combination of the three cannabinoids compared to the control, and compared to pure CBD (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The amount of human CD45+ cells in the bone marrow was significantly decreased in mice treated with the cannabinoid combination compared to pure CBD in the intravenous leukemia model.
source: At the endpoint of the experiment, the amount of human CD45+ cells detected in the bone marrow (BM) was significantly decreased in the mice treated with the combination of the three cannabinoids compared to the control, and compared to pure CBD (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There were no significant differences in the average weight of the mice in the intravenous leukemia model.
source: In this model as well, there were no significant differences in the average weight of the mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD was as effective as the whole extract in the intravenous leukemia model.
source: The combination of 331-18A, CBDV, and CBD was as effective as the whole extract (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The administration of the cannabinoid combination significantly prolonged survival in treated mice compared to the survival of vehicle-treated control mice.
source: In addition, the administration of the cannabinoid combination significantly prolonged survival in treated mice compared to the survival of vehicle-treated control mice (Figure 6H), to a similar degree to the whole extract (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In mice treated with the whole extract, there was a significant reduction in the burden of leukemia in the bone marrow in the PDX model.
source: To examine the clinical relevance, we utilized a patient-derived xenografts (PDX) model with primary cells from a T-ALL patient. After allowing 35 days from transplantation for leukemic cell establishment, mice were treated for 3 weeks with either vehicle or whole extract containing the three cannabinoids. In mice that were treated with the extract, we found a significant reduction in the burden of leukemia in the BM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), peripheral blood (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In mice treated with the whole extract, there was a significant reduction in the burden of leukemia in the peripheral blood in the PDX model.
source: In mice that were treated with the extract, we found a significant reduction in the burden of leukemia in the BM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), peripheral blood (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In mice treated with the whole extract, there was a significant reduction in the burden of leukemia in the spleen in the PDX model.
source: In mice that were treated with the extract, we found a significant reduction in the burden of leukemia in the BM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), peripheral blood (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), and spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The weight of the spleen was significantly lower in extract-treated mice in the PDX model.
source: The weight of the spleen was also significantly lower in extract-treated mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Treatment with the whole extract did not affect the weight of the mice in the PDX model.
source: Treatment with the whole extract did not affect the weight of the mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Targeting Notch signaling components has generated much interest for its therapeutic potential.
source: Targeting Notch signaling components has generated much interest for its therapeutic potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Notch signaling in cancer.

claim: Efforts to develop treatments that target Notch signaling have been unsuccessful so far.
source: However, so far efforts to develop treatments that target Notch signaling have been unsuccessful (Previs et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cannabis is already being prescribed to cancer patients all over the world, mainly as a palliative treatment.
source: Cannabis, in its many forms, is already being prescribed to cancer patients all over the world, mainly as a palliative treatment for the inhibition of nausea and emesis associated with chemotherapy, appetite stimulation, pain relief, and relief from insomnia (Abrams and Guzman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: 331-18A, denoted in the literature as 6,12-dihydro-6-hydroxy-cannabidiol, has not been previously identified in natural and/or decarboxylated Cannabis plants.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, the third phytocannabinoid 331-18A, denoted in the literature as 6,12-dihydro-6-hydroxy-cannabidiol (Stoss and Merrath, 1991), has not been previously identified in natural and/or decarboxylated Cannabis plants.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and citation.

claim: The need for all three cannabinoids for the optimal antitumor effect demonstrates the critical importance of elucidating the individual and polypharmacological effects of the entire molecular spectrum of Cannabis.
source: We suggest that the need for all three cannabinoids for the optimal antitumor effect demonstrates the critical importance of elucidating the individual and polypharmacological effects of the entire molecular spectrum of Cannabis.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The Cannabis plant produces a vast array of over 140 phytocannabinoids and hundreds of other components.
source: The Cannabis plant produces a vast array of over 140 phytocannabinoids and hundreds of other components, but the full extent of their biological effects and interactions is still not completely understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Cannabis composition.

claim: The full extent of the biological effects and interactions of Cannabis components is still not completely understood.
source: The Cannabis plant produces a vast array of over 140 phytocannabinoids and hundreds of other components, but the full extent of their biological effects and interactions is still not completely understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the state of the literature.

claim: Mounting evidence suggests that the combined effect of Cannabis components as a whole is greater than that of each separate compound.
source: Nevertheless, mounting evidence suggests that their combined effect as a whole is greater than that of each separate compound (Russo, 2011; Worth, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A Δ9-THC-rich extract was much more potent than pure Δ9-THC in producing antitumor responses in both cell culture and animal models of breast cancer.
source: Recently, Blasco-Benito et al., 2018, have shown that a Δ9-THC-rich extract was much more potent than pure Δ9-THC in producing antitumor responses in both cell culture and animal models of breast cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Blasco-Benito et al. were unable to identify the combinations of compounds that were responsible for the increased potency of the Δ9-THC-rich extract.
source: However, they were unable to identify the combinations of compounds that were responsible for this increased potency.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Different CBD-rich Cannabis extracts, with equal amounts of CBD but varying concentrations of other minor compounds, led to diverse anticonvulsant effects in a mouse model of epilepsy.
source: In previous publications by our group, we showed that different CBD-rich Cannabis extracts, with equal amounts of CBD but varying concentrations of other minor compounds, led to diverse anticonvulsant effects in a mouse model of epilepsy (Berman et al., 2018), and selective antitumoral effects in Notch1-mutated in T-ALL (Besser et al., 2023), suggesting the potential therapeutic effects of other compounds in the extracts in addition to CBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Different CBD-rich Cannabis extracts led to selective antitumoral effects in Notch1-mutated T-ALL.
source: In previous publications by our group, we showed that different CBD-rich Cannabis extracts, with equal amounts of CBD but varying concentrations of other minor compounds, led to diverse anticonvulsant effects in a mouse model of epilepsy (Berman et al., 2018), and selective antitumoral effects in Notch1-mutated in T-ALL (Besser et al., 2023), suggesting the potential therapeutic effects of other compounds in the extracts in addition to CBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The 'entourage effect' is a mechanism where one compound may synergize the activity and efficacy of another on the same target.
source: A possible mechanism previously suggested to explain the difference between the effects of purified phytocannabinoids versus full-spectrum extracts is the 'entourage effect', where one compound may synergize the activity and efficacy of another on the same target (Russo, 2011; Worth, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 'entourage effect' was postulated by Russo based on a phenomenon observed in the endocannabinoid system by Ben-Shabat et al.
source: This 'entourage effect' was postulated by Russo, 2011, based on a phenomenon observed in the eCBS by Ben-Shabat et al., 1998.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 'entourage effect' is well established for endocannabinoids.
source: While it is well established for endocannabinoids, only very few studies demonstrated this for phytocannabinoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Only very few studies demonstrated the 'entourage effect' for phytocannabinoids.
source: While it is well established for endocannabinoids, only very few studies demonstrated this for phytocannabinoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the state of the literature.

claim: The presence of small amounts of the minor cannabinoids 331-18A and CBDV enhanced the effect of CBD by itself.
source: We showed here that the presence of small amounts of the minor cannabinoids 331-18A and CBDV enhanced the effect of CBD by itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The success in isolating and characterizing a minimal number of cannabinoids that achieve the same antitumor effect as the whole extract is a significant advancement in the field of medical Cannabis.
source: Our success in isolating and characterizing a minimal number of cannabinoids that achieve the same antitumor effect as the whole extract is a significant advancement in the field of medical Cannabis and provides solid evidence for the 'entourage effect'.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The isolation of cannabinoids that achieve the same antitumor effect as the whole extract provides solid evidence for the 'entourage effect'.
source: Our success in isolating and characterizing a minimal number of cannabinoids that achieve the same antitumor effect as the whole extract is a significant advancement in the field of medical Cannabis and provides solid evidence for the 'entourage effect'.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The notion of the 'entourage effect' has been expanded to polypharmaceutical and/or polypharmacological effects.
source: Subsequent reports have expanded the notion of the 'entourage effect' to polypharmaceutical and/or polypharmacological effects, where several of the plant metabolites work simultaneously on the same receptors, and/or when the same molecule has several different targets within the same system (Mechoulam and Ben-Shabat, 1999; Russo, 2018; Di Marzo and Piscitelli, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CBD has been shown to present complex signaling capabilities of many receptors in the extended endocannabinoid system.
source: CBD has been shown to present complex signaling capabilities of many receptors in the extended eCBS.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about CBD.

claim: CBD has a weak affinity to CB2.
source: Specifically, it was shown to have a weak affinity to CB2, and a strong affinity to many of the TRPV family receptors, including TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 (Kis et al., 2019; De Petrocellis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CBD has a strong affinity to many of the TRPV family receptors, including TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3.
source: Specifically, it was shown to have a weak affinity to CB2, and a strong affinity to many of the TRPV family receptors, including TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 (Kis et al., 2019; De Petrocellis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The known cannabinoids CBD and CBDV affected both CB2 and TRPV1.
source: More specifically, the known cannabinoids CBD and CBDV affected both, while the novel 331-18A exerted its effect only through CB2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The novel 331-18A exerted its effect only through CB2.
source: More specifically, the known cannabinoids CBD and CBDV affected both, while the novel 331-18A exerted its effect only through CB2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Following the stimulation of CB2 and TRPV1 receptors, Ca2+ is depleted from the ER and there is an increase in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: Following the stimulation of the receptors, Ca2+ is depleted from the ER and there is an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ and activation of eIF2α followed by ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Stimulation of CB2 and TRPV1 leads to activation of eIF2α followed by ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 signaling.
source: Following the stimulation of the receptors, Ca2+ is depleted from the ER and there is an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ and activation of eIF2α followed by ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The upregulation of CHAC1 inhibits the S1 furin-like cleavage of Notch1 at the Golgi apparatus.
source: The upregulation of CHAC1 inhibits the S1 furin-like cleavage of Notch1 at the Golgi apparatus (Chi et al., 2012), leading to the arrival of immature Notch1 to the plasma membrane as we have previously shown (Besser et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and previous work by the authors.

claim: Inhibition of the Notch1 pathway ultimately leads to apoptosis in T-ALL cells that rely on mutated Notch1 for propagation.
source: This inhibition of the Notch1 pathway ultimately leads to apoptosis in T-ALL cells that rely on mutated Notch1 for propagation (see schematic representation in Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and schematic representation in Figure 7.

claim: The potential antitumor effects of cannabinoids through the Notch1 signaling pathway were previously demonstrated in glioma, where THC induced the expression of p8 protein, upstream to ATF3/4.
source: The potential antitumor effects of cannabinoids through the Notch1 signaling pathway were previously demonstrated in glioma, where THC induced the expression of p8 protein, upstream to ATF3/4 (Carracedo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The activation of Notch signaling by ER stress was demonstrated in Alzheimer's disease, polycystic ovary syndrome, and other types of cancer.
source: The activation of Notch signaling by ER stress was demonstrated in additional systems, including Alzheimer's disease (Ohta et al., 2011), polycystic ovary syndrome (Koike et al., 2023), and other types of cancer (Izrailit et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A previous work suggested a role for ER stress in Notch1 cleavage and leukemia cell death through the inhibition of proteasome activity in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
source: A previous work that focused on chronic lymphocytic leukemia suggested a role for ER stress in Notch1 cleavage and leukemia cell death through the inhibition of proteasome activity (Rosati et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Blocking Notch1 maturation through the eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 pathway and inhibiting the S1 furin-like cleavage of Notch1 have the potential to affect all types of activation mutations in Notch1.
source: These findings suggest blocking Notch1 maturation through the eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 pathway and inhibiting the S1 furin-like cleavage of Notch1 have the potential to affect all types of activation mutations in Notch1, and also all four human homologs of Notch (Notch1-4) (Chi et al., 2012; Mungrue et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: Blocking Notch1 maturation through the eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 pathway has the potential to affect all four human homologs of Notch (Notch1-4).
source: These findings suggest blocking Notch1 maturation through the eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP-CHAC1 pathway and inhibiting the S1 furin-like cleavage of Notch1 have the potential to affect all types of activation mutations in Notch1, and also all four human homologs of Notch (Notch1-4) (Chi et al., 2012; Mungrue et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: Treatment with the extract containing the three cannabinoids reduced leukemic burden in a PDX model.
source: To validate the clinical relevance of our findings for patients, we tested the extract containing the three cannabinoids in an in vivo PDX model (Jung et al., 2018; Richter-Pechańska et al., 2018; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and demonstrated treatment reduced leukemic burden.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Medical Cannabis is already routinely prescribed to cancer patients.
source: As medical Cannabis is already routinely prescribed to cancer patients, tailoring chemovars that contain the appropriate cannabinoids to T-ALL patients can provide them with optimal care that offers anti-cancer properties on top of the palliative ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about medical Cannabis use.

claim: Tailoring chemovars that contain the appropriate cannabinoids to T-ALL patients can provide them with optimal care that offers anti-cancer properties on top of the palliative ones.
source: As medical Cannabis is already routinely prescribed to cancer patients, tailoring chemovars that contain the appropriate cannabinoids to T-ALL patients can provide them with optimal care that offers anti-cancer properties on top of the palliative ones.
